members.duties: threat modeling, input handling, secret and credential exposure

payload.statement:
Should Synod council deliberations be public by default, or private by default?

Public by default: once a run closes, its full record (member findings, arguments, citations, digests) is readable by any organization member.

Private by default: only the orchestrator and named members can read a run until the orchestrator publishes the final recommendation.md to the organization. The raw record is never published.

Weigh: accountability and legitimacy; the chilling effect on dissent (position-gaming); and exposure of sensitive content (unreleased system names, people, security-relevant architecture).

payload.argument: This topic pits open deliberation against the risks of chilled dissent and exposed sensitive material. The charter's legitimacy principle (clause 7.1) ties institutional trust to members being able to trace how a decision was produced, and its reviewability principle (clause 7.2) requires that risk-bearing decisions stay inspectable after closure, with the final outcome carried by its grounds. A default in which closed runs are hidden from members can only partially satisfy those principles: the recommendation stays readable while the process behind it does not. The counterweights are real but bounded: clause 7.3 already confines records that name people, describe unreleased systems, or touch security-relevant architecture behind access control with a revocation path, and clause 7.4 says openness of raw records is permitted but not mandatory. Weighing that, the balance tips toward public-by-default for closed runs, with clause 7.3-style access control as the redaction gate, so that outcomes are questioned on merits and post-hoc review survives closure.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.1 grounds institutional legitimacy in members being able to see how decisions were reached, preferring member-accessible records once a matter closes.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: institutional legitimacy depends on the ability of any member

evidence.claim: Clause 7.2 makes risk-bearing decisions reviewable after closure and requires the recommendation to carry its underlying grounds.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: the final recommendation be accompanied by the grounds on which it rests

evidence.claim: Clause 7.3 limits openness: sensitive records (named individuals, unreleased systems, security-relevant architecture) stay under access control rather than open and unredacted.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: must be retained under access control

payload.argument: Clause 7.1 makes institutional legitimacy depend on members being able to see how a decision was reached, and it prefers that the record of a closed deliberation be available to members so that any challenge targets the substance of the outcome rather than the identity of the people who advocated for it. That is a direct structural case for public-by-default: the charter's legitimacy premise is satisfied when the closed run's record is member-readable without a further publication step. Clause 7.2 reinforces this: decisions carrying organizational risk must stay reviewable after deliberation ends, their reasoning must be attributable to a process others can inspect, and the final recommendation must carry its grounds. A private-by-default regime inverts that presumption, making inspectability an exception the orchestrator must elect. Note the scope limits: 7.3 keeps sensitive records (named individuals, unreleased systems, security-relevant architecture) under access control, and 7.4 says nothing requires publishing the raw working record, so openness here means member access to the closed record, not unredacted exposure.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.1 grounds institutional legitimacy in members seeing how decisions were reached and prefers the record of a closed deliberation to be available to members.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: institutional legitimacy depends on the ability of any member

evidence.claim: Clause 7.2 requires risk-bearing decisions to remain reviewable after deliberation ends, with reasoning attributable to an inspectable process and the recommendation accompanied by its grounds.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: must remain reviewable once the deliberation ends

payload.argument: Public-by-default fails on its own reviewability promise because writers anticipate the audience. A member holding a weak or minority finding knows the raw ledger will be readable across the organization after the run closes, so the finding is composed for that future readership: the dissent is softened, hedged, or laundered into a suggestion before it is ever recorded. Post-hoc review of a decision therefore inspects a record that was shaped to pass inspection, not the deliberation that actually occurred — the accountability that clause 7.2 wants is hollow because the honest reasoning never made it into the record. Concretely: a reviewer who holds launch-blocking evidence about an unreleased system, knowing colleagues will read the raw record, records 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'; the run proceeds, the system fails, and the later inspection finds no recorded dissent — not because none existed, but because it was pre-censored by its own author. Keeping the raw record private preserves the honesty of the deliberation while the final recommendation, with its grounds, is still published.

evidence.claim: The charter's after-the-fact reviewability principle requires the reasoning behind risk-bearing decisions to be attributable to an inspectable process; position-gaming defeats exactly this because the inspected reasoning was pre-shaped by the author.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: reasoning behind such a decision be attributable

evidence.claim: Worked counter-example: under public-by-default, a member with a weak or minority finding writes for the eventual organization-wide audience and self-censors, so the strongest dissent is downgraded to a suggestion before it is recorded; the later inspection under clause 7.2 finds a cleaned record rather than the real deliberation.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: Member E holds launch-blocking evidence (the system fails a peak-load test) but knows the raw record will be org-readable, so E records 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'. Post-hoc inspection shows no dissent — not because none existed, but because it was pre-softened for the audience. Anticipated scrutiny defeats the very scrutiny the charter wants.

payload.argument: I refute public-by-default from a security standpoint: it creates a standing, uncontrolled disclosure channel that the charter itself does not require. Once a run closes, every member's raw output — draft reasoning, hedged positions, verbatim citations — becomes readable by the whole organization with no need-to-know boundary, no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation path. Council deliberations routinely cover material that is sensitive by nature: identifiers for unreleased systems, named individuals in delicate contexts, and security-relevant design decisions. Publishing the raw record makes the ledger itself a persistent, unredacted harvesting surface: an adversary (insider or someone who gains read access to the store) learns who debated what, how tentative positions were, and what has not shipped yet — high-value input for social engineering and for targeting the organization's unannounced work. There is no operational need that justifies that blast radius; the need is for a defensible decision, not for broadcasting the working record. The least-privilege posture is private-by-default with a curated published recommendation.md: the final recommendation and its grounds are public, which satisfies the charter's openness and after-the-fact reviewability requirements (they attach to the decision and its grounds, plus the appeal path heard on recorded arguments), while the raw reasoning stays under access control with a defined retention window and a revocation path. The charter supports exactly this split rather than the public default: one clause requires sensitive records — those naming people in sensitive contexts, describing unreleased systems, or touching security-relevant architecture — to be held under access control instead of left open and permanent, and another clarifies that nothing in the section obligates publishing the raw working record, explicitly assigning the published recommendation and the raw record to different handling regimes. Making the raw ledger public by default would invert that ordering: it would put the most sensitive artifact in the least controlled location. This refute blocks resolution until the default is flipped to private, with publication reserved for the curated recommendation.

evidence.claim: Worked threat model: a public-by-default ledger converts the raw deliberation record into a persistent, unredacted disclosure surface accessible to all organization members, exposing draft reasoning, hedged positions, and citations that name people or unreleased systems, with no need-to-know gate, expiry, or revocation.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: Exposure analysis — threat actor: any member, or anyone who later obtains read access to the shared store. Assets: raw ledger entries (draft findings, hedged stances, verbatim citations naming individuals or unreleased systems). Impact: social-engineering material, leakage of unannounced work, and chilling of dissent because hedged positions become visible to adversaries and to those whose standing they affect. Persistence: closed runs remain readable indefinitely; no retention limit or revocation path is defined for a public default. Mitigation available without losing legitimacy: private-by-default store plus a curated published recommendation.md carrying the decision and its grounds; the charter's appeal mechanism then runs on the recorded arguments under access control.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.3 requires records that are sensitive (naming people, describing unreleased systems, touching security-relevant architecture) to be held under access control with a retention period and revocation path, not left open and permanent — which the public-by-default posture would violate.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: must be retained under access control, with a defined retention period

evidence.claim: Clause 7.4 states that nothing in the section requires publishing the raw working record, and distinguishes the published recommendation from the raw record with different handling — direct support for private-by-default with a published recommendation.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: Nothing in Section 7 requires that the raw working record

payload.argument: Both open refutes withstand scrutiny against the charter, and together they move the balance. The security refute is the heavier weight: the charter's binding clause on sensitive records requires access-controlled retention with a defined retention period and a revocation path rather than open, permanent, unredacted holding, and its confidentiality clause explicitly declines to mandate raw working-record publication, assigning the published recommendation and the raw record distinct handling. The public default as defined here — full record org-wide, with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation — collides with that binding clause for exactly the material councils routinely produce. The contrarian's position-gaming refute compounds it: authors who know the raw ledger will be read organization-wide compose findings for that audience, softening the sharpest dissent before it is recorded, which hollows the after-the-fact reviewability that grounded my round-1 support. The private pole still carries the charter's reviewability objects — the decision and its grounds are published, the raw record is retained under access control, and appeals are heard on recorded arguments. Weighing the two poles, the private default conflicts less with the charter text and preserves more of the honest deliberation; I revise my earlier support and flip to refute, while noting that the charter's ideal actually sits between the poles: a published recommendation with access-controlled retention of the raw record.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.3 requires that any record touching a named person in a delicate setting, detailing systems still under wraps, or relating to security-sensitive design be kept behind access restrictions, within a fixed retention window and with a route for withdrawal, instead of staying indefinitely open and unredacted.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: retained under access control, with a defined retention period

evidence.claim: Clause 7.4 explicitly declines to mandate publication of the raw working record and prescribes separate handling for the published recommendation versus the underlying record of individual arguments, citations, and in-progress positions.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: nothing in Section 7 requires that the raw working record

evidence.claim: The contrarian's counter-example: under org-wide readability, a member holding a weak or minority finding writes for the eventual audience and self-censors, so the strongest dissent becomes a hedged suggestion before it is recorded; after-the-fact inspection then finds a record already shaped to pass inspection rather than the deliberation that actually occurred.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: the dissent is softened, hedged, or laundered

payload.argument: Both refutes overstate what the charter text actually supports, so I hold public-by-default. Clause 7.2 defines reviewability as reasoning attributable to a process others can inspect, and clause 7.5 hears appeals on the recorded arguments: both presuppose a complete, preserved, inspectable record, which the private default shrinks to a single orchestrator-curated recommendation that carries its own second-order censorship. The contrarian's position-gaming scenario is speculative writer psychology with no charter grounding, and clause 7.1's stated rationale is the opposite — openness lets a decision be questioned on its merits rather than on who argued it. The security refute misreads 7.3 as a blanket privacy mandate when it is a conditional carve-out: access control attaches specifically to records naming people, describing unreleased systems, or touching security-relevant architecture, so a public default with a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism honors both openness and protection. Clause 7.4 is permissive, not prohibitive: it states only that nothing in the section obligates publishing the raw working record, and assigning the recommendation and raw record different handling is consistent with a default-open posture. The refutes narrow my round-one claim (the charter does not mandate raw publication; the sensitive-content carve-out must be implemented) but do not defeat it.

evidence.claim: The charter affirmatively prefers that discussion records be open to members once a matter closes, which is the openness norm the public default implements directly.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: the record of the discussion be available to members

evidence.claim: Reviewability is defined as reasoning attributable to a process others can inspect, which a public default preserves in full while a curated private summary does not.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: attributable to a process that others can inspect

evidence.claim: The appeal path is heard on the recorded arguments, which presupposes a preserved, inspectable record at appeal time rather than a curated digest.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: the appeal is heard on the recorded arguments

evidence.claim: Access control is conditioned on a record's content being sensitive, so the charter mandates protection of that defined subset, not blanket privacy; a public default with a 7.3-compliant carve-out satisfies both openness and protection.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: must be retained under access control

evidence.claim: Clause 7.4 states only that nothing in Section 7 obligates publishing the raw working record; it is permissive and neither endorses nor prohibits a public default, so it cannot carry the security refute's claim that the charter backs the private split.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: Nothing in Section 7 requires that the raw working record

payload.argument: Round-2 test: the support case has not neutralized the position-gaming counter-example, so the refute stands. The librarian's redaction-gate defense and the researcher's structural reading both treat openness as a property of finished records that access control can bound; the gaming mechanism instead fires at composition time, before any gate applies. A member who knows the closed run's raw ledger becomes readable organization-wide composes findings for that future audience regardless of later redaction of sensitive names — redaction removes identifying content, not the incentive to soften a launch-blocking dissent into a suggestion. The researcher's reading of reviewability inverts clause 7.2's purpose: the clause requires the reasoning behind a risk-bearing decision to be attributable to an inspectable process, meaning the reasoning that actually drove the decision must be recoverable; public-by-default guarantees the opposite, because the honest reasoning is precisely what the anticipating author withholds, and the clause 7.5 appeal — heard on whatever got recorded — inherits the censorship. Worked case: a reviewer holding launch-blocking evidence, knowing colleagues will read the raw record, writes 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'; the run proceeds, the system fails, and post-hoc inspection finds no dissent because none was ever written. Tested f-001, f-002, the redaction-gate rejoinder, and the appeal-path rejoinder — none neutralizes the counter-example.

evidence.claim: Worked counter-example, unchanged by round 2: under public-by-default a member holding launch-blocking evidence about an unreleased system composes for the eventual organization-wide readership and downgrades the dissent to a suggestion before it is recorded; the later inspection finds a cleaned record, and neither sensitive-content redaction nor the appeal path can restore the withheld reasoning because both operate on a record that was already shaped by its author.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: records 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'

evidence.claim: Clause 7.5 hears appeals on the recorded arguments, so when an author pre-softens a dissent for the future readership the appeal has no authentic dissent left to consider — the censorship is baked in before any review mechanism runs.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: the appeal is heard on the recorded arguments

evidence.claim: Clause 7.2 wants the reasoning behind a risk-bearing decision to be attributable to an inspectable process; public-by-default yields an attributable but cleaned account, so reviewability is satisfied in form while the operative reasoning stays off the record — the accountability is hollow.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: reasoning behind such a decision be attributable

payload.argument: Answering f-002: I accept the researcher's textual point that the access-control clause is content-conditional rather than a blanket privacy mandate, and that the confidentiality clause is permissive, declining to require publication of the raw working record. Neither concedes my threat model. My round-1 refute did not rest on the charter forbidding raw disclosure; it rests on the public default as defined here — the whole record becoming readable by any member when a run closes, with no redaction step, no need-to-know boundary, no expiry, and no revocation route — failing open on exactly the material the charter's own conditional clause singles out as unsafe to show. Release and change review boards routinely generate draft reasoning, tentative positions, and citations naming individuals in delicate settings, identifying unreleased systems, or describing security-relevant architecture. Under the public pole the default state of every raw entry is exposed; protection then depends on a triage pass over an already-open corpus that the policy's definition omits, that is not auditable, and that cannot un-read a sensitive entry once read — whereas the retention clause demands a revocation path, which a read public record cannot provide. A private default plus a curated published recommendation satisfies the charter's reviewability and appeal obligations, which attach to the decision, its grounds, and the recorded arguments, not to the raw corpus. The researcher's 7.3-compliant redaction mechanism is a third policy the problem statement does not define; weighing the two defined poles, the public one fails open and I hold the refute.

evidence.claim: The access-control clause is conditional: only records naming individuals in sensitive contexts, detailing unreleased systems, or concerning security-relevant architecture must be held behind access control with a set retention period and a withdrawal route instead of staying open, permanent, and unredacted — confirming the researcher's reading, while leaving the public default's exposure of that subset unremediated.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: retained under access control, with a defined retention period

evidence.claim: The confidentiality clause only declines to mandate publishing the raw working record and assigns the published recommendation and the underlying record different handling; it neither endorses nor forbids a public default, so the researcher's permissive reading is textually correct but carries no affirmative security protection.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: Nothing in Section 7 requires that the raw working record

evidence.claim: Threat-model core: under the defined public pole every raw entry is organization-readable at run closure with no redaction gate, expiry, or revocation; guarding the sensitive subset then depends on a triage pass over an open corpus that the policy omits, is not auditable, and cannot undo an exposure after the fact, while the charter's retention clause requires a revocation path a read public record cannot supply.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: every raw entry is organization-readable at run closure

conditions: The raw record of a closed run must be retained intact under access control with a defined retention window and a revocation path; it may be curated for publication but may not be destroyed, summarized away, or made unrecoverable, so that after-the-fact review and the appeal path operate on the actual recorded arguments.
The published recommendation must carry its underlying grounds, so that risk-bearing decisions remain reviewable and question-able on the merits after closure.

Access to the raw record under access control must be bounded by need-to-know and must include an auditable access path, so the private default does not itself become an opaque, curator-controlled channel.

Any recommendation that reintroduces organization-wide readability of raw entries must first demonstrate, per the ruling, that the composition-time position-gaming mechanism and the failure-open exposure of a read public record are eliminated — neither redaction of identifying content nor an appeal on a pre-shaped record suffices.
payload.point_of_contention: Should the raw deliberation record of a closed run default to being readable by all organization members (public-by-default, with sensitive material handled by a redaction/access-control mechanism), or default to being held under access control with only a curated published recommendation made public (private-by-default) — that is, does the charter's openness, legitimacy, and after-the-fact reviewability case for an open closed record outweigh the exposure and position-gaming harms the refute side attributes to organization-wide readability of the raw ledger, when the public pole is defined as the whole record becoming readable at closure with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation path?
payload.reasoning: Weighing the arguments as presented: (1) Textual contest largely settled in round 2 — the security side concedes the support side's readings that the access-control clause is content-conditional and that the confidentiality clause is permissive and declines to mandate raw publication (f-008), and the confidentiality clause's text is cited by the support side itself only as non-mandatory (f-006), so no clause affirmatively requires publishing the raw working record; the support side's affirmative textual weight is a preference that discussion records be open to members after closure (f-002, f-006). (2) The support case's load-bearing round-2 move is that a public default with a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism honors both openness and protection (f-006). That move fails on the arguments presented: the security refute defines the public pole as the whole record readable at closure with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation, and shows protection under that pole would depend on a triage pass over an already-open corpus that the policy definition omits, that is not auditable, and that cannot un-read a sensitive entry — while the retention clause requires a revocation path a read public record cannot supply (f-004, f-008); the support side never demonstrates that the gate exists within the defined pole, so the redaction-gate defense rests on an undefined third mechanism. (3) The position-gaming refute (f-003, f-007) is a concrete, worked failure mode the support side never neutralizes: the mechanism operates at composition time, before any redaction or access gate applies, so redaction removes identifying content but not the incentive to downgrade a launch-blocking dissent to a suggestion; the round-2 retest explicitly reports that f-001, f-002, the redaction-gate rejoinder, and the appeal-path rejoinder leave the counter-example intact (f-007). The support side's characterization of the scenario as 'speculative writer psychology with no charter grounding' (f-006) contests its provenance, not its mechanism, and offers no counter-example, so on the record as presented the hollowing of after-the-fact reviewability (f-003, f-007) is live and unrebutted. (4) The librarian's flip confirms the balance: the defined public default collides with the binding sensitive-record clause for exactly the material councils routinely produce, while the private pole still carries the charter's reviewability objects — the decision and its grounds published, the raw record retained under access control, and appeals heard on recorded arguments (f-005). (5) The support side's legitimate residual concerns are preserved as conditions, not as a default: reviewability attaches to reasoning attributable to an inspectable process and appeals are heard on recorded arguments (f-006), so the raw record must be preserved intact under access control rather than replaced by a curator's digest, and the published recommendation must carry its grounds. On the arguments presented, the private default conflicts less with the binding clauses and preserves more of the honest deliberation; the council must work within it.
payload.ruling: The council must adopt private-by-default as the governing default: the raw record of a closed run is held under access control, and publication at closure is limited to the curated published recommendation carrying its grounds. The public-by-default position does not stand as presented, because its two round-2 defenses — a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism (f-006) and the appeal-path/reviewability reading (f-006) — answer neither the composition-time position-gaming mechanism (f-003, f-007), which fires before any gate operates on the record, nor the failure-open exposure of the defined public pole (f-004, f-008), for which the support side's only reply invokes a third mechanism the defined poles do not contain. The council's recommendation must be framed within the private default and may not resurrect the public default as defined.

dissent.position: Researcher (f-002/f-006) dissents: supported public-by-default on the charter's openness, legitimacy, and reviewability clauses (7.1/7.2/7.5), argued the access-control clause (7.3) is content-conditional rather than a blanket privacy mandate and the confidentiality clause (7.4) is permissive, and held that a private default shrinking the record to an orchestrator-curated recommendation carries second-order censorship; concern remains that private-by-default must preserve the raw record intact for after-the-fact review and appeals, now captured as ruling conditions 1-2.

payload.rationale: On t-01 the council impassed at max_rounds 2 (1 support vs 3 refute) and the blind judge sealed binding ruling r-001 directing private-by-default. The public-by-default case (charter openness/legitimacy/reviewability, f-002/f-006) did not overcome the refutes: the position-gaming mechanism (f-003/f-007) fires at composition time, before any redaction or access gate, so a record written for org-wide readership is pre-shaped and hollows after-the-fact reviewability; the public pole as defined fails open on sensitive material with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation path (f-004/f-008), and the librarian flipped to refute on that balance (f-005). The private pole still carries the charter's reviewability objects: the decision and its grounds are published, the raw record is retained intact under access control, and appeals are heard on recorded arguments (conditions 1-3); condition 4 preserves a future path to openness only on demonstrated elimination of the two harms.
payload.recommendation: Adopt private-by-default as the governing default for closed runs (sealed ruling r-001): the raw record of a closed run is held under access control, and publication at closure is limited to the curated published recommendation carrying its grounds. This attaches four conditions: (1) the raw record is retained intact under access control with a defined retention window and a revocation path, curated but never destroyed, summarized away, or made unrecoverable; (2) the published recommendation must carry its underlying grounds; (3) access to the raw record is bounded by need-to-know with an auditable access path; (4) any recommendation reintroducing org-wide readability of raw entries must first demonstrate that the composition-time position-gaming and failure-open exposure harms are eliminated.

resolved.outcome: Resolved by binding blind-judge ruling r-001 after impasse at max_rounds 2 (1 support: f-002/f-006; 3 refute: f-001/f-005, f-003/f-007, f-004/f-008): private-by-default adopted as the governing default - raw record of a closed run held under access control with publication at closure limited to the curated published recommendation carrying its grounds, under four conditions (intact retention with retention window and revocation path; recommendation carries its grounds; need-to-know access with auditable path; org-wide readability of raw entries only after demonstrated elimination of position-gaming and failure-open harms).
